newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan oil monopoly seeks price rises.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan oil monopoly seeks price rises.

text.p: Taiwan state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Wednesday it was seeking government permission to raise oil prices, but would not confirm reports it wanted increases of up to 10 percent.
"We (have) already send our request to the (economic) ministry to set up a committee to review our oil prices," an official of the state-run giant told Reuters by telephone.
Such a committee could be expected to review the price-hike proposal within a week, with an emphasis on the inflationary effect of any increase, she said.

Energy analysts agreed with Taipei media reports that the monopoly had applied to boost prices by up to 10 percent to address operating shortfalls blamed for November's pre-tax loss of T$1.129 billion (US$41 million).
Chinese Petroleum can adjust prices by no more than three percent a month without state energy commission approval.
Government and private economists said a 10 percent rise in petrol prices would cause the consumer price index to jump by about 0.43 percent in the month it takes effect.
The wholesale price index would jump 0.53 percent.
Taiwan consumer prices rose a year-on-year 3.19 percent in November, while wholesale prices fell an annual 3.02 percent, continuing a downward trend seen in recent months.
Prices fell on Taiwan's stock exchange on Wednesday, in part due to worries that an oil price hike would spark inflation.
Chinese Petroleum's 95-octane petrol now sells for T$16.7 per litre (US$2.29 per gallon) at filling stations, including a T$0.2 per litre air-pollution surcharge.
Chinese Petroleum reported a cumulative budget deficit of T$8.126 billion for the July-November period.
Chinese Petroleum's November loss contrasted sharply with its targeted pre-tax profit of T$1.438 billion, a reversal blamed mainly on higher-than-expected world oil prices.
Chinese Petroleum's November oil import costs averaged US$22.13 per barrel, much higher than the budgeted US$15.26 per barrel, according to figures disclosed by the company.
The oil monopoly imported 12.8 million barrels in November, bringing the cumulative total since the July 1 fiscal year start to 91.7 million barrels, the figures showed.
Taiwan, almost totally dependent on foreign crude, imports more than 150 million barrels a year.
